MlxOSBrix.NativeFirst: brixOS may use its own handle, wait, memory-map, process and IPC primitives.
MlxOSBrix.PosixFacade: std.posix translates required POSIX semantics onto brixOS native primitives.
MlxOSBrix.WaylandTransport: brixOS must provide a Wayland-capable byte-stream transport with ancillary handle/fd passing semantics, shared memory object export/import, and poll/wait integration. The public Mlx Wayland API remains identical across Linux, BSD and brixOS.

Principles.Rule: Every kernel resource a process uses is an object it holds by a handle; nothing is reached by a global number (a pid, a signal number, a descriptor number) without a handle.
There is one way to wait: for any of a set of handles to reach a state, with a deadline.
The kernel keeps no hidden cursor: a read or write names its position, or says it streams.

A process learns of what happens to it (an interrupt from its terminal, a child that ended, a fault) as events it takes from its own queue; code runs asynchronously only through the one upcall the process registers.
Copy on write is the system's way to copy: files, trees (snapshots), volumes and processes (branch) are copied by sharing pages.

The Linux system call numbers are served by a separate layer of the kernel (its own number space) that translates them onto these objects; nothing in the kernel's core names a Linux number, structure or signal.

CallingConvention.Rule: SYSCALL with the call number in rax, at or above NATIVE_BASE (0x4000); the arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8, r9.
The result in rax: a value (zero or more), or a negative Status.
Numbers below NATIVE_BASE are Linux's (the translation layer). A process may use both while std moves over.

Status.note: returned negated; std turns them into Mlx error sets
Status.Code: the handle's object does not do that
the other end of a stream or channel is closed
the upcall ran during the call
a table is full (handles of a process)
too many links on the way
a link or rename across volumes

Handles.Rule: A handle is a non-zero 32-bit value naming an entry of the process's handle table: an object and the rights the entry carries. 0 is no handle.
A handle names the entry as it was when the handle was made (its generation): once closed, the handle stays invalid even when the entry is used again.
Rights only shrink: duplicate gives the same object with a subset of the rights; a handle sent over a channel moves with its rights.
Handles.Rights: read write wait duplicate transfer control
Handles.Kinds: process group node stream channel session memory timer socket

States.note: a 32-bit word per object; wait watches it
States.Bit: a read would not block (a stream or channel has data, a node, a session with input for its front group, a timer that expired)
a process ended; a group has no process left
a process has a change to take (a child ended, stopped or went on)
a process has events in its queue
a group: it is in front of the session

Wait.WaitItem: handle: u32, want: u32 (state bits), seen: u32 (written: the state when the call returned), reserved: u32
Wait.Rule: The call returns as soon as one item's state has a wanted bit, with every item's seen word filled; 0 and timed_out when the deadline (monotonic nanoseconds, 0: do not block, all ones: none) passes first.
A process waiting is woken by the state change itself; nothing polls.

upcall_return(context*)

clock_read(clock) -> nanoseconds (0 monotonic, 1 real time)

timer_create(deadline, period) -> h (deadline on the monotonic clock, period 0: once; readable once it expired; a streaming read of 8 bytes takes how many times it expired since the last read, waiting for the deadline; 0 bytes when it will not expire again)

snapshot(source directory h, directory h, path, length, flags) (a copy of the tree the handle names at path, its files sharing their pages; flags: read-only 1; the disk's volume into /volumes is a snapshot on the disk, read-only only)

node_map(file h, offset, size) -> address (the file's pages mapped as the caller's, shared until a write copies one: a private view; the file does not change)
socket_open(kind) -> h (a socket: stream 1 (TCP), datagram 2 (UDP), ping 3 (ICMP echo); kind socket)
socket_bind(socket h, port) (0: one the system picks)
socket_connect(socket h, address*) (address: 4 bytes IPv4, port u32; a stream's connection begins: WRITABLE when made, PEER_GONE when it failed; a datagram socket's peer)
socket_listen(socket h)
socket_accept(socket h, peer* or 0) -> h (would_block: none yet; the listener is READABLE when one waits)
socket_send(socket h, data, length, address* or 0) -> count (would_block: none taken; a datagram's destination, or the peer)
socket_receive(socket h, data, capacity, from* or 0) -> count (0: the peer closed; would_block: nothing yet)
socket_info(socket h, into*) (local address, peer address, the pending error (a Status code, taken), connected)

session_pair(handles*) -> 0 (a terminal of its own: handles[0] its control side, a stream: what programs write to the session is read there, what is written there is typed; handles[1] the session, kind session, for the programs; the control side's reads wait for output, its state READABLE when there is some)
session_size(session or control h, columns, rows) (the terminal's size in cells, what the window size asked by TIOCGWINSZ is)

system_info(buffer, capacity) -> count (the machine's figures as words: memory bytes, free bytes, processors, uptime ns, page faults served, system calls, switches between processes, the devices' message-signalled interrupts taken, then the waits for the kernel in ns: all processors' summed, the longest since the boot, what held the kernel then (the process id above 32 bits; below, 0x80000000 and a system call's number, or an interrupt's or fault's vector), the longest since last asked and its holder (taking these starts that anew); how many there are, the first `capacity` written)
identity_set(user, group) (the caller's identity, which its children inherit; a process of user 0 may take any, another only its own: no_right)
node_own(h, user, group) (the node's owner and group, all ones: as it is; user 0 may give a node away, its owner may change its group alone)

channel_peer(channel h, into*) (who holds the other end: the process that made or opened it, pid, user, group, name length (u32 each), then its program's leaf name up to 64 bytes; a bus learns a client's identity and app so)

listener_make(directory h, path, length, mode) -> h (a listener node: opening it gives the opener a channel of its own and sends its far end to this handle as a message with no bytes and one handle; would_block when the listener has not taken the earlier ones, peer_gone when its end is closed; the node goes with node_remove)

process_start(records*, capacity) -> count (the caller's handles by role, as (role u32, handle u32) records: input 1, output 2, errors 3, directory 4 (its working directory at the start), session 5, a spawner's own from 16; the count of them all, the first `capacity` written)

Events.Rule: An event is a record (kind, sender's process id, detail) in the receiving process's queue; its state has the events bit while the queue is not empty.
Events.Kind: Ctrl-Z at the session, or a request
a stopped process goes on; always also done
a child has a change to take
detail: the fault and its address; delivered at once, through the upcall only
the process read its session from a group that is not in front
the session's size changed, urgent data
one the program and its senders give a meaning (the detail)
a write to a stream whose reader is gone
Events.Rule: events_take writes records of four u32: kind, detail, sender (a process id; 0 the kernel), reserved (a fault: the low half of its address).

A process that has claimed no kind and set no upcall sees its events through the Linux layer's view (signals), as the programs built for Linux expect; one that has, sees them as events. A fault such a process has not claimed still goes to a handler it has in the Linux layer's view for the fault's signal (a crash report installed there stays the program's when it claims other kinds).
An event kind the program has not claimed takes its default. A claimed one stays in the queue for the program; with an upcall set, the kernel runs it.

The upcall: the interrupted registers and SSE state are saved in a context record on the upcall's stack, entry(context*) runs, upcall_return(context*) goes back. No second upcall starts before the first returns; a call the upcall interrupted returns interrupted.
There are no per-kind handlers, masks or numbers in the kernel: std.posix builds sigaction, sigprocmask and signal numbers on the queue and the one upcall.

Processes.Rule: A program starts with a start block: its arguments, its environment and its handles by role (input, output, errors, working directory, session, and any the spawner adds). The arguments and environment are on its stack; process_start gives the roles, which a branch copies and a replace's start block sets anew.
process_spawn starts a program in a new process with exactly the handles given. process_branch copies the caller (copy on write, as snapshots copy trees); std.posix's fork is a branch.

The first process is /system/programs/impulse when the archive has it (else flux), with the serial console as its input, output, errors and session; it alone may call system_power. It starts the services of /system/settings/init/services with process_spawn and roles, answers impulsectl on the FIFO /temporary/init/control, and shows the boot on a display with ignition on two streams.

All of the machine's memory is the kernel's to hand out (mapped at its start beyond the GiB the boot tables map); system_info says how much there is and is free, with the processors, the uptime and the kernel's counts, for a program that sizes its work by them (std.build's runner).
The mouse is /devices/mouse: the PS/2 mouse's bytes as they come (three a packet, the first with bit 3 set), a read waiting for them.

The display is /devices/framebuffer: a read gives its geometry (width, height, bytes a row, format: four words), node_map its pixels (32 bits each, blue first). The keyboard is /devices/keyboard: its scancodes (set 1) as they come, a read waiting for them. A virtual console is a program on both with a session pair (mlx-console).

A group is an object: processes join it; a session (a terminal) has a front group, which gets its interrupt, quit and suspend events and may read it. A streaming read of the session from a group behind sends that group read_behind and waits (the processes stop and read again when they go on); io_error when the event would not reach the reader.

Personality.Rule: A process has an identity, a user and a group: the first process's is 0, spawn and branch pass it on, replace keeps it, identity_set changes it (down from 0 for good). A node has an owner and a group (node_make gives the maker's; node_own changes them) and a mode, which decide what a process may do with it; user 0 may do anything. The login (sentinel) branches, takes the person's identity and replaces itself with their session; the accounts are /system/settings/users, groups and shadow.

The Linux layer (kernel/linux) takes the numbers below NATIVE_BASE: descriptors are its view of handles, signals its view of events (SIGINT the interrupt event, SIGTSTP suspend, SIGCHLD child, rt_sigframes its view of the upcall), errno its view of Status.
